newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil soars, then falls on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil soars, then falls on profit-taking.

text.p: Heating oil prices soared again Thursday on worries over low inventories in the United States and Europe as Western oil companies and consumers start preparing for the coming winter, but the market was unable to hold on to its gains.

Heating oil for October delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange gained more than 1 cent to 72.80 cents a gallon Thursday after rising 2.08 cents on Wednesday. October's gain was the highest since November 1991 after the Gulf War.
But a rush by speculators late in the day to cash in profits led to heavy selling pressure and October closed down 0.87 cent at 70.90 cents.
"We had gained four cents in the last two days, so we were due for some profit-taking," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc.
November crude oil fell 30 cents to $24.16 a barrel, partly because of the late selling pressure in heating oil, and October gasoline fell 0.11 cent a gallon at 62.99 cents.
Heating oil has risen more than 25 percent in the last three months on worries over tight supplies in the United States and Europe. The surge has helped boost prices of crude and gasoline.
"I think people are expecting a hard winter, with strong demand and supplies low," one trader said.
Industry and government reports this week showed heating oil and diesel stocks were about 30 percent below 1995 levels in the Northeast, the nation's largest market for home heating oil.
Stocks in Europe's biggest market, Germany, were also well below normal.

In addition, the markets are doing without several hundred thousand barrels of oil a day from Iraq after a U.N.-backed oil-for-food deal was put on hold indefinitely after Baghdad's military incursion into Kurdish areas earlier this month.
In other markets, improved weather forecasts for the Midwest harvest pushed down corn and soybean prices.
At the Chicago Board of Trade November soybeans closed down 5 cents a bushel at $7.90-3/4 and December corn ended 6-1/4 cents lower at $3.06.

Traders also said soybean oil prices were hit by a statement from EuroCommerce, a group that represents the retail and wholesale sector in 20 European countries, that the U.S. risked a boycott of its soybean shipments this year unless it agreed to label which beans had been genetically altered.
About three percent of U.S. soybeans this year have been planted from transgenic seed, altered to increase plant strength on fields where Monsanto Co.'s popular herbicide Roundup is used.
October soybean oil closed 0.35 cent per pound lower at 24.56 cents.
Gold prices slumped after news the International Monetary Fund may sell 5 million ounces of gold from its 104 million ounce reserves to help the world's poorest nations.
December gold at the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division ended down $1.70 an ounce at $383.60 an ounce, after falling to a three-year low at $382.60 an ounce early.
IMF head Michel Camdessus said the IMF had the necessary 85 percent majority needed to pass the gold plan. But U.S. Treasury Secretary Rubin said the sales may not be needed until the year 2000.
"The IMF has probably had the needed majority in favour of selling some gold for some time, but it may not happen for some time," Paine Webber commodities research director Bernard Savaiko said.
"The real reason gold has been on the defensive is the lack of inflation and the relative attraction of stock and bond markets for investors," Savaiko said.
